column4: Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has succeeded; this is the closest nonlexical formulation of the source’s Godfearing person being moved aside from the blaze.
Abraham asks God, وَٱجْنُبْنِى, to keep him and his sons away from worshipping idols; the source root ج ن ب retains its causative sense of making a person stand apart from danger.
Believers are told to avoid intoxicants, gambling, sacrificial stones, and divining arrows so that they may succeed; ٱجْتَنِبُوهُ turns stepping aside from a snare into a commanded path to safety.
The command to avoid the pollution of idols and false speech uses the source’s ج ن ب family for deliberate removal from what corrupts.
Those who avoid false powers rather than worship them and turn back to God receive good news; withdrawal from the false object is paired with orientation toward God.

Every community received the call to worship God and avoid false powers, after which the ayah contrasts those God guided with those upon whom error became due; stepping aside divides the two outcomes.
Avoiding the major sins brings expiation and an honorable entrance, so an active use of the ج ن ب family leads beyond danger to a safe destination.
The believers are characterized by avoiding major sins and indecencies and forgiving when angered; the source root describes a sustained moral position away from ruin.
Those who avoid the major sins and indecencies, apart from minor lapses, stand within the Lord’s vast forgiveness; avoidance is linked to mercy rather than mere spatial distance.
Satan urges a person to disbelieve and then disowns him once he does, giving another specific instance of a companion leading someone toward ruin and abandoning him at the edge.
The tempter and the tempted end together eternally in the Fire, completing 59:16’s false companionship with the destination it concealed.
The wrongdoer wishes he had not taken a certain person as an intimate friend, echoing the garden-dweller’s recognition that a companion nearly caused his fall.
The regretted companion led him away from the Reminder after it reached him, and Satan proves deserting; this identifies diversion from guidance as the mechanism of the fall in 25:28.
Whoever blinds himself to the Merciful’s remembrance is assigned a satan as a close companion, joining the section’s heedlessness to the dangerous companion scene.
Those companions bar people from the path while the people suppose themselves guided, making the plunge’s blindness a false confidence about direction.
On coming before God, the misled person wishes an east-to-west distance separated him from the companion; only at the destination does he perceive how far the companion pulled him off course.
Regret cannot help because wrongdoer and companion share the punishment, completing the hidden companionship trap of 43:36–38.
The angels ask God to protect the believers from evil deeds and say that whoever is protected that Day has received mercy; divine protection removes both the cause and outcome of the fall.
The garden-dwellers taste no further death and God protects them from Hell’s punishment, restating the completed safety of one drawn away from fire.
God protects the righteous from the evil of that Day and grants radiance and joy; removal from danger opens into the positive state beyond it.
Israel is warned not to transgress over its good provision lest wrath descend, and whoever incurs that wrath has fallen; moral excess, downward movement, and ruin are made explicit.
Satan causes the pair to slip from the garden, brings them out of their state, and they are told to descend; deceptive prompting becomes an actual downward displacement.
After the command to descend, God promises that whoever follows His guidance will neither stray nor suffer; guidance marks the route that prevents descent from becoming ruin.
Noah’s son trusts a mountain to protect him from the water, but no protector exists from God’s decree and the wave takes him; apparent physical height cannot arrest the fatal descent.
People are asked whether they feel secure from the earth suddenly swallowing them; the unnoticed ground can become the pit beneath a confident walker.
Those who plot evil are asked whether they feel secure from God causing the earth to swallow them or punishment arriving unexpectedly; heedless security stands directly over a hidden fall.
Those delivered to land are asked whether they feel secure from being swallowed into it or struck by a storm with no guardian, repeating the brink hidden beneath ordinary safety.
The deniers are confronted with the earth below and sky above: God could make the earth swallow them or drop a fragment of sky; ruin can open in either vertical direction.
Punishment covers the wrongdoers from above and from beneath their feet, turning the root-family suggestion of a foot snare into complete vertical enclosure.
A barrier is set before and behind the rejecters and they are covered so they cannot see; blindness and confinement make continued movement itself perilous.
The condemned man is given extensive wealth, identifying the worldly resource that precedes the punitive ascent announced in 74:17.
Despite abundant gifts, he greedily desires still more; possession does not change his direction and instead prepares the burden that follows.
God will burden him with a punishing ascent, صَعُودًا; upward motion here is torment, a sharp reversal that prevents the section’s moral ascent from being reduced to mere height.
God says He will make the rejecter burn in Saqar, using a ص ل ي verb after the wealthy man’s false security and punitive climb.
The people of the right ask the criminals what put them into Saqar, opening the explanation of the fiery destination named in 74:26.
The criminals say they did not feed the needy, making refusal of the steep ascent’s feeding act one stated cause of their fiery destination.
The person God leaves to stray experiences a constricted chest as though laboriously climbing into the sky; ascent becomes suffocation when it lacks guidance.
Whoever turns away from the Lord’s remembrance is driven into an escalating, arduous punishment; this difficult “ascent” reverses the source’s upward call.
The transgressor prefers the nearer life, naming the desire that governs the downward course whose destination appears in 79:39.
Hell is the refuge of the one who transgresses and prefers worldly life, completing the first direction of the choice in 79:38.
The person who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the soul from desire takes the opposite course from the desire-follower who falls in 20:16.
The Garden becomes the refuge of the one who restrains desire, completing the safe direction opposite 79:39’s Hell.
People prefer the nearer worldly life, a low and immediate orientation set beneath the Most High named at the surah’s opening.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, clarifying the enduring destination toward which glorifying the Most High and answering the upward call are directed.
Those who spent and struggled before the victory are greater in degree than later spenders, explicitly turning expenditure into an elevated rank.
Some desert Arabs treat their spending as means of nearness to God and the Messenger’s prayers; wealth given away becomes actual approach rather than failed protection.
People do not attain true righteousness until they spend from what they love, making relinquishment of cherished wealth the upward passage into virtue.
The denier violently repulses the orphan, reversing the steep ascent’s movement toward the vulnerable person.
He does not urge feeding the needy, supplying the exact neglected act opposite the ascent’s feeding scene.
The reproached people do not honor the orphan, beginning a wealth passage whose conduct runs opposite to the section’s ascent.
They do not encourage one another to feed the needy, directly negating one of the steep ascent’s defining acts.
They consume inheritance voraciously, showing wealth taken inward rather than released toward another person.
They love wealth with consuming love, identifying the attachment that cannot save when the ground of judgment gives way.
The earth is crushed repeatedly, converting the preceding false security in wealth into a scene where stable ground itself collapses.
Hell is brought forth and the human finally remembers, but remembrance then cannot benefit; recognition arrives only after the downward choice is irreversible.
The condemned person wishes he had sent something ahead for his life, recognizing too late that wealth had to be given forward rather than held as protection.
The condemned person did not encourage feeding the needy, adding a withheld ascent-act to the useless wealth and burning already described in 69:28–31.
The criminal would ransom himself from that Day with his children, beginning the exhaustive proof that no possessed human resource can stop the fiery outcome in 70:15.
He would surrender his spouse and brother as ransom, extending the failed attempt to arrest ruin through what is closest to him.
He would offer the clan that sheltered him, so even the social protection once surrounding him cannot pull him away.
He would offer everyone on earth if that could save him, exhausting all imaginable ransom immediately before the ayah rejects escape and names the blaze.
Those who do not answer their Lord would offer all the earth and as much again as ransom, yet face the bad reckoning and Hell; total possession cannot purchase removal from the end.
If the wrongdoers owned everything on earth and its equal, they would offer it against the Day’s punishment, showing wealth’s complete impotence only when ruin becomes visible.
Every wrongdoing soul would offer all the earth as ransom on seeing the punishment, a repeated formulation of possession failing at the decisive instant.
No ransom is accepted from hypocrites or disbelievers, and the Fire is their refuge; the failed payment and fiery destination are explicitly joined.
Disbelievers spend wealth to bar others from God’s path, but their spending becomes regret, defeat, and gathering into Hell; expenditure pointed in the wrong direction cannot become ascent.
Those who hoard gold and silver rather than spend in God’s way are warned of painful punishment, setting stored wealth against the section’s purifying gift.
The hoarded metal is heated in Hell and used to brand its owners, so the possession meant as security becomes the instrument of burning.
Solomon writes, “Do not exalt yourselves over me; come to me in submission”; self-height from the ع ل و root is answered by a summons that requires surrender.
Pharaoh and his chiefs respond arrogantly to Moses and Aaron and are called a people who were عَالِينَ; height names oppressive refusal rather than nearness to God.
God rescues Israel from Pharaoh’s humiliating torment and calls Pharaoh high-handed and excessive; the oppressor’s عَالِي status is set against divine rescue from beneath it.
Few believe Moses for fear of persecution because Pharaoh is high-handed in the land and excessive; claimed earthly height functions by pushing others down.
Israel is warned that it will corrupt twice and rise to great self-exaltation, using عُلُوًّا for a height whose very form invites judgment.
God is glorified and exalted in immense height above what people falsely attribute to Him, reserving true عُلُوّ for God rather than human claimants.
Because God is the Truth and what is invoked besides Him is false, the ayah names God as the High and Great; true height is explicitly bounded against false worship.
The repeated declaration that God is Truth, rival invocations are false, and He is the High and Great reinforces who alone owns the section’s upward pole.
The heavenly servants fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded, giving divine height an answering posture of obedience rather than self-elevation.
Pharaoh proclaims his Egyptian kingdom and points to rivers flowing beneath him, staging his false lordship through an earthly above-and-below hierarchy.
When Pharaoh’s people provoke God, all are drowned, turning the ruler who boasted of waters beneath him into one overwhelmed by water.
Abraham’s opponents propose building a structure and casting him into a blaze, deliberately constructing the fiery trap whose direction God reverses in 37:98.
They intend a plot against Abraham, but God makes them the lowest, explicitly bringing the would-be burners down instead.
The disbelievers ask to see the human and jinn misleaders so they can put them beneath their feet among the lowest; the companions who caused error are assigned the downward place.
The command to prostrate and draw near shows bodily lowering as the act of spiritual approach, a corrective reversal within the section’s vertical axis.
Those who believe, migrate, and strive with wealth and lives are greater in rank with God, making devoted use of wealth an explicit elevation.
Those who strive with wealth and lives are favored by a degree over those who sit back, again attaching upward rank to the active surrender of possessions.
The ayah says the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preferment than worldly differentiation, relocating true elevation beyond present possessions.
God distributes livelihoods and raises people over one another in degrees for mutual service, yet His mercy is better than what they amass; worldly height and accumulation are expressly relativized.
God makes people successors on earth and raises some in degrees over others to test them in what He has given, turning possession and rank into examination rather than rescue.
God is the Raiser of degrees and Lord of the Throne, locating the power to confer true height in the same divine source toward which the section turns.
The Event is “abasing, raising,” compressing the section’s two directions into the final reversal by which some are lowered and others elevated.
Faces on that Day are humbled, establishing the lowered human pole of a passage that ends in fire.
Those humbled faces enter an intensely hot fire, joining abasement to the same burning destination as the source’s downward course.
Other faces on that Day are joyful, beginning the opposed outcome to the humbled faces of 88:2.
Those joyful faces are in a lofty garden, making their final abode explicitly high in contrast to the lowered faces and fire.
Everyone is brought to Hell according to the Lord’s decree, establishing the perilous threshold from which 19:72 specifically saves the Godfearing.
The attendants are told to guide the wrongdoers and their associates to the path of Hell, a terrible counter-image in which “guidance” directs companions downward.
The believing man asks why he calls his people to salvation while they call him to the Fire; the rival calls state the section’s two directions without metaphor.
His people call him to deny God and associate what he does not know, while he calls them to the Mighty, Forgiving One; the content of each direction in 40:41 is made explicit.
Pharaoh and his chiefs are made leaders who call to the Fire and receive no help on Judgment Day, presenting false leadership as a downward summons.
The associators call toward the Fire, while God calls toward the Garden and forgiveness; the section’s opposed directions become two explicit invitations.
God calls to the abode of peace and guides whom He wills to a straight path, stating the safe destination of the true call in positive terms.
The ayah asks whether one cast into the Fire is better or one who comes secure on Resurrection Day, directly setting involuntary fiery descent against safe arrival.
Whoever brings a good deed receives better and is secure from that Day’s terror, supplying the protected counterpart to the face-first casting in 27:90.
The disbelievers are driven in groups to Hell until its gates open, giving the downward company and destination opposite the Godfearing group in 39:73.
Those who feared their Lord are conducted in groups to the Garden, setting the Godfearing person’s destination opposite the fiery route without relying on possessions.
